v.why: At high learning rates, larger batches damp the gradient noise that drives instability, whereas elsewhere the lost steps dominate.
Under standard parameterization wide nets take larger function-space steps per update, so raising the learning rate destabilizes them first.
Strong L2 on every layer compounds multiplicatively across depth, collapsing signal through the added layer.
When width is the capacity bottleneck, an extra layer supplies missing expressivity that wide nets do not need.
Wide nets carry the most surplus capacity, so added L2 removes excess fit rather than useful fit.
sklearn divides the L2 term by the minibatch size, so tiny batches amplify the effective penalty and raising alpha over-regularizes.
Large batches leave few steps in the epoch budget, so a larger learning rate is needed to converge.
Large updates compound through stacked ReLU layers, so adding a layer at high learning rate destabilizes training.
With few optimizer steps, the harder-to-train deeper net cannot reach its potential within the epoch budget.
At tiny learning rates wider nets move further in function space per Adam step, converting width directly into faster fitting.

I dropped two hypotheses whose condition is the edited field's own value: learning_rate_init up conditioned on learning_rate_init low, and alpha up conditioned on alpha high. None of the rest merely switches off the edited component.

From the remaining 18, I kept one per edit-and-condition pair and avoided repeating a mechanism:
- I dropped the step-count versions of batch_size against learning_rate_init (#1 and #19). They overlap with the learning-rate-at-large-batch hypothesis, and the noise-damping version is more open to debate.
- I dropped batch_size up under high alpha and alpha up under high batch_size. Both use the same sklearn penalty-scaling argument as alpha up under small batches.
- I dropped width up when depth is high, which mirrors the depth-and-width capacity argument already kept.
- I dropped learning_rate_init down when depth is high, which repeats the depth-instability-at-high-learning-rate argument.
- I dropped learning_rate_init up when batch_size is low (instability from noise) and when width is low (the reverse of the wide-net hypothesis I kept).
